paragraphs: “Those cultivated parents put this poor five-year-old through every torture you can think of. They beat her, thrashed her, kicked her for no reason at all, until her whole body was one bruise. Then they moved on to subtler cruelty. They shut her up all night in the freezing cold, in an outhouse. She didn’t ask to be let out in the night (as if a five-year-old, sleeping her sound, angelic sleep, could be trained to wake up and ask!). So they smeared her face with filth and stuffed it into her mouth, and it was her mother, her own mother, who did this. And that mother could sleep while she heard the poor child groaning! Can you understand why a little creature who can’t even grasp what is being done to her should beat her aching little chest with her tiny fist, in the dark and the cold, and weep her meek, unresentful tears to ‘dear, kind God’ to protect her? Do you understand that, my friend and brother, you pious, humble novice? Do you understand why this infamy has to exist and is allowed to? They tell me that without it man couldn’t have lived on earth, because he wouldn’t have known good and evil. Why should he know that diabolical good and evil when it costs so much? The whole world of knowledge isn’t worth that child’s prayer to ‘dear, kind God’! I say nothing of the suffering of grown-up people. They have eaten the apple, damn them, and the devil take them all! But these little ones! I’m making you suffer, Alyosha. You’re not yourself. I’ll stop if you like.”
“Never mind. I want to suffer too,” muttered Alyosha.

“One more picture, only one, because it’s so curious and so characteristic, and I’ve only just read it in some collection of Russian antiquities. I’ve forgotten the name. I’ll have to look it up. It was in the darkest days of serfdom, at the beginning of the century, and long live the Liberator of the People! In those days there was a general with aristocratic connections, the owner of vast estates. He was one of those men (somewhat exceptional even then, I believe) who retire from the service and are convinced that it has earned them absolute power over the lives of their subjects. There were such men then. So this general settles on his property of two thousand souls and lives in grand style. He lords it over his poor neighbors as if they were hangers-on and jesters. He keeps kennels with hundreds of hounds and nearly a hundred dog-boys, all mounted and in uniform. One day a serf-boy, a little child of eight, throws a stone in play and hurts the paw of the general’s favorite hound. ‘Why is my favorite dog lame?’ He is told that the boy threw a stone and hurt the dog’s paw. ‘So you did it.’ The general looks the child up and down. ‘Take him.’ They take him. They take him from his mother and keep him locked up all night. Early next morning the general rides out in full hunting parade, with the hounds, his dependents, dog-boys and huntsmen, all mounted around him. The house servants are called together to be edified, and in front of them all stands the child’s mother. The child is brought out of the lock-up. It’s a gloomy, cold, foggy autumn day, a capital day for hunting. The general orders the child to be undressed. The boy is stripped naked. He shivers, numb with terror, not daring to cry.... ‘Make him run,’ commands the general. ‘Run! run!’ shout the dog-boys. The boy runs.... ‘At him!’ yells the general, and he sets the whole pack of hounds on the child. The hounds catch him and tear him to pieces before his mother’s eyes!... I believe the general was afterwards declared unfit to manage his estates. Well, what did he deserve? To be shot? To be shot, to satisfy our moral feelings? Speak, Alyosha!”
“To be shot,” murmured Alyosha, raising his eyes to Ivan with a pale, twisted smile.
“Bravo!” cried Ivan, delighted. “If even you say so.... You’re a fine monk! So there’s a little devil sitting in your heart, Alyosha Karamazov!”
“What I said was absurd, but—”

“That’s just the point, that ‘but’!” cried Ivan. “Let me tell you, novice, the absurd is all too necessary on earth. The world stands on absurdities, and perhaps nothing would have happened in it without them. We know what we know!”
“What do you know?”

“I understand nothing,” Ivan went on, as if in delirium. “I don’t want to understand anything now. I want to stick to the fact. I decided long ago not to understand. If I try to understand anything, I’ll be false to the fact, and I’ve made up my mind to stick to the fact.”
“Why are you testing me?” Alyosha cried, suddenly distressed. “Will you finally say what you mean?”
“Of course I will. That’s what I’ve been leading up to. You’re dear to me, I don’t want to let you go, and I won’t hand you over to your Zossima.”
Ivan was silent for a minute, and his face suddenly became very sad.

“Listen! I took up the case of children only to make my argument clearer. About the other tears of humanity, which soak the earth from its crust to its core, I will say nothing. I’ve narrowed my subject on purpose. I’m a bug, and I admit in all humility that I can’t understand why the world is arranged as it is. Men are to blame themselves, I suppose. They were given paradise, they wanted freedom, and they stole fire from heaven, though they knew they would be made unhappy. So there’s no need to pity them. With my pitiful, earthly, Euclidian understanding, all I know is that there is suffering and that no one is guilty; that cause follows effect, simply and directly; that everything flows and finds its level. But that’s only Euclidian nonsense, I know that, and I can’t agree to live by it! What comfort is it to me that no one is guilty, that cause follows effect simply and directly, and that I know it? I must have justice, or I will destroy myself. And not justice in some remote, infinite time and space, but here on earth, where I could see it myself. I have believed in it. I want to see it, and if I’m dead by then, let me rise again, because if it all happens without me, that will be too unfair. Surely I haven’t suffered just so that I, with my crimes and my sufferings, can manure the soil of a future harmony for somebody else. I want to see with my own eyes the hind lie down with the lion and the victim rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it has all been for. All the religions of the world are built on this longing, and I am a believer. But then there are the children, and what am I to do about them? That’s a question I can’t answer. For the hundredth time I repeat: there are masses of questions, but I’ve taken only the children, because in their case what I mean is unanswerably clear. Listen! If everyone must suffer to pay for the eternal harmony, what have children to do with it? Tell me, please. It’s beyond all comprehension why they should suffer, and why they should pay for the harmony. Why should they, too, be raw material to enrich the soil for somebody’s future harmony? I understand solidarity in sin among men. I understand solidarity in retribution, too. But there can be no such solidarity with children. And if it’s really true that they must share the responsibility for all their fathers’ crimes, then that truth is not of this world and is beyond my comprehension. Some jester will say, perhaps, that the child would have grown up and sinned. But you see, he didn’t grow up. He was torn to pieces by the dogs, at eight years old. Oh, Alyosha, I’m not blaspheming! I understand, of course, what an upheaval of the universe it will be when everything in heaven and earth blends in one hymn of praise, and everything that lives and has lived cries aloud: ‘You are just, O Lord, for Your ways are revealed.’ When the mother embraces the fiend who threw her child to the dogs, and all three cry aloud with tears, ‘You are just, O Lord!’ then, of course, the crown of knowledge will be reached and everything will be made clear. But here is what stops me: I can’t accept that harmony. And while I’m on earth, I hurry to take my own measures. You see, Alyosha, perhaps it really may happen that if I live to that moment, or rise again to see it, I, too, may cry aloud with the rest, looking at the mother embracing the child’s torturer, ‘You are just, O Lord!’ But I don’t want to cry it then. While there’s still time, I hurry to protect myself, and so I renounce the higher harmony altogether. It’s not worth the tears of that one tortured child, who beat her little chest with her little fist and prayed in her stinking outhouse, with unatoned tears, to ‘dear, kind God’! It’s not worth it, because those tears are unatoned for. They must be atoned for, or there can be no harmony. But how? How will you atone for them? Is it possible? By avenging them? But what do I care about avenging them? What do I care about a hell for the oppressors? What good can hell do, when those children have already been tortured? And what becomes of harmony, if there is a hell? I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don’t want any more suffering. And if the sufferings of children go to swell the sum of suffering that was needed to pay for the truth, then I protest that the truth isn’t worth such a price. I don’t want the mother to embrace the oppressor who threw her son to the dogs! She has no right to forgive him! Let her forgive him for herself, if she wants to. Let her forgive the torturer for the immeasurable suffering of her own mother’s heart. But the sufferings of her tortured child she has no right to forgive. She can’t forgive the torturer, even if the child were to forgive him! And if that’s so, if they have no right to forgive, what becomes of harmony? Is there in the whole world a being who would have the right to forgive, and could? I don’t want harmony. Out of love for humanity I don’t want it. I would rather be left with the unavenged suffering. I would rather stay with my unavenged suffering and unsatisfied indignation, _even if I were wrong_. Besides, too high a price is being asked for harmony. It’s beyond our means to pay so much to get in. And so I hurry to give back my entrance ticket, and if I’m an honest man, I’m bound to give it back as soon as possible. And that is what I’m doing. It’s not God that I don’t accept, Alyosha. It’s only that I most respectfully return Him the ticket.”
“That’s rebellion,” murmured Alyosha, looking down.

“Rebellion? I’m sorry you call it that,” said Ivan earnestly. “One can hardly live in rebellion, and I want to live. Tell me yourself, I challenge you, answer me. Imagine that you are building the fabric of human destiny with the aim of making people happy in the end, of giving them peace and rest at last. But to do it, you have to torture to death just one tiny creature, that baby beating her chest with her fist, for instance, and found that edifice on her unavenged tears. Would you agree to be the architect on those conditions? Tell me, and tell the truth.”
“No, I wouldn’t agree,” said Alyosha softly.

“And can you accept the idea that the people you’re building it for would agree to take their happiness on the foundation of the unatoned blood of a little victim? And that, having accepted it, they would stay happy for ever?”

“No, I can’t accept it. Brother,” said Alyosha suddenly, with flashing eyes, “you just asked whether there is a being in the whole world who would have the right to forgive, and could. But there is a Being, and He can forgive everything, all and for all, because He gave His innocent blood for all and for everything. You’ve forgotten Him, and on Him the edifice is built, and it is to Him they cry aloud, ‘You are just, O Lord, for Your ways are revealed!’”

“Ah! The One without sin, and His blood! No, I haven’t forgotten Him. On the contrary, I’ve been wondering all along why you didn’t bring Him in sooner, because in arguments on your side people usually put Him in the foreground. Do you know, Alyosha, and don’t laugh, I made a poem about a year ago. If you can spare me another ten minutes, I’ll tell it to you.”
“You wrote a poem?”

“Oh, no, I didn’t write it,” laughed Ivan, “and I’ve never written two lines of poetry in my life. But I made up this poem in prose, and I remembered it. I was carried away when I made it up. You’ll be my first reader, or rather listener. Why should an author give up even one listener?” smiled Ivan. “Shall I tell it to you?”
“I’m all attention,” said Alyosha.
“My poem is called ‘The Grand Inquisitor.’ It’s a ridiculous thing, but I want to tell it to you.”
